items.stem: Electric wires have a coating of PVC or rubber because:
items.answer: it is a poor conductor and prevents shocks
items.markingKey: (b) it is a poor conductor and prevents shocks.

items.stem: Which of these is a metal that is liquid at room temperature?
items.answer: mercury
items.markingKey: (a) Mercury is a metal that is liquid at room temperature. The others: bromine – a non-metal that is liquid at room temperature; graphite – a non-metal that is a good conductor of electricity; caesium – a metal with a melting point so low that it melts in the palm.

items.stem: Why is sodium kept immersed in kerosene oil?
items.answer: It reacts so vigorously with oxygen and moisture in air that it catches fire; kerosene keeps air away.
items.markingKey: 1 mark reactivity. 1 mark keeps air away.

items.stem: Classify these elements as a non-metal or a metal: sodium, bromine, aluminium, phosphorus, mercury.
items.answer: A non-metal: bromine, phosphorus. A metal: aluminium, mercury, sodium.
items.markingKey: ½ mark per correctly placed item (rounded): A non-metal: bromine, phosphorus. A metal: aluminium, mercury, sodium.

items.stem: Classify these elements as a non-metal or a metal: nitrogen, phosphorus, zinc, bromine, gold.
items.answer: A non-metal: bromine, nitrogen, phosphorus. A metal: gold, zinc.
items.markingKey: ½ mark per correctly placed item (rounded): A non-metal: bromine, nitrogen, phosphorus. A metal: gold, zinc.

items.stem: A copper vessel turned green after a few days. A student cleaned it with lemon juice. Explain the green coating and the cleaning, with equations where possible.
items.answer: Copper reacts with moist CO₂ in air to form green basic copper carbonate [CuCO₃·Cu(OH)₂]. Lemon juice (citric acid) reacts with this basic coating and dissolves it, so the shine returns.
items.markingKey: 1 mark coating. 1 mark acid. 1 mark basic nature.

items.answer: A is true, but R is false.

items.stem: Which term is described here? "Producing a ringing sound when struck."

items.stem: Does copper give hydrogen gas with dilute hydrochloric acid? Give a reason.
items.answer: No, it does not displace hydrogen; copper is below hydrogen in the reactivity series.
items.markingKey: 1 mark answer. 1 mark reason.

items.stem: Why is a layer of aluminium oxide useful to aluminium?
items.answer: The thin, tough oxide layer protects the metal from further oxidation (corrosion).
items.markingKey: 2 marks.

items.stem: Arrange these metals in decreasing order of reactivity: gold, lead, iron, aluminium.
items.answer: aluminium > iron > lead > gold
items.markingKey: Reactivity series: K > Na > Ca > Mg > Al > Zn > Fe > Pb > [H] > Cu > Hg > Ag > Au.

items.stem: A strip of magnesium is placed in silver nitrate solution. Will any reaction occur? If yes, write the equation.
items.answer: Yes. Mg + 2AgNO₃ → Mg(NO₃)₂ + 2Ag. Magnesium is more reactive than silver.
items.markingKey: 1 mark yes/no with reason (reactivity series). 1 mark equation.

items.stem: A strip of iron is placed in silver nitrate solution. Will any reaction occur? If yes, write the equation.
items.answer: Yes. Fe + 2AgNO₃ → Fe(NO₃)₂ + 2Ag. Iron is more reactive than silver.
items.markingKey: 1 mark yes/no with reason (reactivity series). 1 mark equation.

items.stem:
Read: Rohan put zinc strips in four test tubes containing copper sulphate, silver nitrate, iron(II) sulphate and magnesium sulphate solutions.
(i) In which tube does a reddish-brown deposit form? Write the equation. (ii) What colour does the solution in that tube become? (iii) In which tube(s) does no reaction occur, and why? (iv) Arrange magnesium, zinc, iron, copper and silver in decreasing order of reactivity.
items.answer: (i) Copper sulphate: Zn + CuSO₄ → ZnSO₄ + Cu. (ii) Colourless. (iii) Magnesium sulphate: zinc is less reactive than magnesium. (iv) Mg > Zn > Fe > Cu > Ag.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each part.

items.stem: Metals A, B, C and D were added to solutions. A displaced B from its salt; C did not react with B's salt; D displaced A from its salt. Arrange them in decreasing order of reactivity.
items.answer: D > A > B > C (C is below B).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each comparison; 1 mark order.

items.stem: Which term is described here? "A freshly prepared mixture of concentrated hydrochloric acid and concentrated nitric acid in the ratio 3:1 that dissolves gold and platinum."
items.answer: aqua regia
items.markingKey: (a) Aqua regia is a freshly prepared mixture of concentrated hydrochloric acid and concentrated nitric acid in the ratio 3:1 that dissolves gold and platinum.

items.stem: A strip of magnesium is placed in copper sulphate solution. Will any reaction occur? If yes, write the equation.
items.answer: Yes. Mg + CuSO₄ → MgSO₄ + Cu. Magnesium is more reactive than copper.
items.markingKey: 1 mark yes/no with reason (reactivity series). 1 mark equation.

items.stem: Zinc metal will displace the metal from which of these solutions?
items.answer: copper sulphate solution
items.markingKey: (d) Reactivity series: K > Na > Ca > Mg > Al > Zn > Fe > Pb > H > Cu > Hg > Ag > Au. A metal displaces only less reactive metals from their salt solutions.

items.stem: Magnesium metal will displace the metal from which of these solutions?
items.answer: zinc sulphate solution

items.answer: sodium > lead > copper > gold

items.stem: Zinc metal will NOT displace the metal from which of these solutions?
items.answer: potassium nitrate solution

items.stem: Define an electrovalent bond.
items.answer: The bond formed by the electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions
items.markingKey: 1 mark: An electrovalent bond – the bond formed by the electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions.

items.stem: What is the formula of sodium fluoride?
items.answer: NaF
items.markingKey: (d) Valency of Na = 1, of F = 1: NaF.

items.stem: Show the formation of potassium chloride from potassium (Z = 19) and chlorine (Z = 17) by transfer of electrons. Write the formula and the number of electrons transferred per formula unit.
items.answer: Potassium (2, 8, 8, 1) loses 1 electron to form K+; chlorine (2, 8, 7) gains 1 to form Cl−. Formula KCl; 1 electron transferred.
items.markingKey: 1 mark configurations and ions. 1 mark formula and electrons.

items.stem: Show the formation of magnesium oxide from magnesium (Z = 12) and oxygen (Z = 8) by transfer of electrons. Write the formula and the number of electrons transferred per formula unit.
items.answer: Magnesium (2, 8, 2) loses 2 electrons to form Mg2+; oxygen (2, 6) gains 2 to form O2−. Formula MgO; 2 electrons transferred.
items.markingKey: 1 mark configurations and ions. 1 mark formula and electrons.

items.stem: Show the formation of potassium sulphide from potassium (Z = 19) and sulphur (Z = 16) by transfer of electrons. Write the formula and the number of electrons transferred per formula unit.
items.answer: Potassium (2, 8, 8, 1) loses 1 electron to form K+; sulphur (2, 8, 6) gains 2 to form S2−. Formula K₂S; 2 electrons transferred.
items.markingKey: 1 mark configurations and ions. 1 mark formula and electrons.

items.stem: Why do ionic compounds not conduct electricity in the solid state?
items.answer: The ions are held in fixed positions in the crystal and cannot move.
items.markingKey: 1 mark fixed ions. 1 mark no movement.

items.stem: Show the formation of aluminium oxide from aluminium (Z = 13) and oxygen (Z = 8) by transfer of electrons. Write the formula and the number of electrons transferred per formula unit.
items.answer: Aluminium (2, 8, 3) loses 3 electrons to form Al3+; oxygen (2, 6) gains 2 to form O2−. Formula Al₂O₃; 6 electrons transferred.
items.markingKey: 1 mark configurations and ions. 1 mark formula and electrons.

items.stem: Show the formation of potassium oxide from potassium (Z = 19) and oxygen (Z = 8) by transfer of electrons. Write the formula and the number of electrons transferred per formula unit.
items.answer: Potassium (2, 8, 8, 1) loses 1 electron to form K+; oxygen (2, 6) gains 2 to form O2−. Formula K₂O; 2 electrons transferred.
items.markingKey: 1 mark configurations and ions. 1 mark formula and electrons.

items.stem: Define electrolytic refining.
items.answer: Purification of an impure metal by electrolysis, using the impure metal as anode and a thin strip of pure metal as cathode
items.markingKey: 1 mark: Electrolytic refining – purification of an impure metal by electrolysis, using the impure metal as anode and a thin strip of pure metal as cathode.

items.stem: Which of these metals is found free (native) in nature?
items.answer: silver
items.markingKey: (b) Silver is found free (native) in nature. The others: mercury – extracted by heating the sulphide ore in air alone; magnesium – extracted by electrolysis of the molten chloride or oxide; copper – extracted by heating the sulphide ore in air alone.

items.stem: Explain why mercury can be extracted from cinnabar simply by heating.
items.answer: Mercury is low in the reactivity series; heating HgS in air gives HgO (2HgS + 3O₂ → 2HgO + 2SO₂), which decomposes on further heating (2HgO → 2Hg + O₂).
items.markingKey: 1 mark low reactivity. 1 mark equations.

items.stem: Classify these metals by method of extraction, extracted by heating the sulphide ore in air alone or found free (native) in nature: mercury, gold, copper.
items.answer: Extracted by heating the sulphide ore in air alone: copper, mercury. Found free (native) in nature: gold.
items.markingKey: ½ mark per correctly placed item (rounded): Extracted by heating the sulphide ore in air alone: copper, mercury. Found free (native) in nature: gold.

items.stem: Classify these metals by method of extraction, extracted by heating the sulphide ore in air alone or extracted by reduction of the oxide using carbon: copper, zinc.

items.markingKey: ½ mark per correctly placed item (rounded): Extracted by heating the sulphide ore in air alone: copper. Extracted by reduction of the oxide using carbon: zinc.

items.stem: Why is the reactivity of a metal related to how easily it is extracted? Give one example each of a metal extracted by electrolysis, by carbon reduction and by heating alone.
items.answer: More reactive metals hold oxygen more strongly, so they need more energy (electrolysis); less reactive ones are reduced easily. Electrolysis: Na/Al; carbon: Zn/Fe; heating alone: Hg/Cu.
items.markingKey: 1 mark relation. 2 marks examples.

items.stem: Which term is described here? "Heating a carbonate ore strongly in limited air to convert it into an oxide."
items.answer: calcination
items.markingKey: (c) Calcination is heating a carbonate ore strongly in limited air to convert it into an oxide.

items.stem: An element X forms an oxide X₂O₃ that reacts with both HCl and NaOH. X is found as a protective oxide layer that prevents its corrosion. Identify X, write both reactions of the oxide, and say how X is extracted.
items.answer: X is aluminium. Al₂O₃ + 6HCl → 2AlCl₃ + 3H₂O; Al₂O₃ + 2NaOH → 2NaAlO₂ + H₂O. Extracted by electrolysis of molten alumina.
items.markingKey: 1 mark X. 1 mark reactions. 1 mark extraction.

Read: A jeweller in Thrissur makes ornaments of 20-carat gold. Pure gold is too soft. Brass and bronze vessels are also sold in the market, and the iron gate of the shop is galvanised.
(i) What percentage of a 20-carat ornament is gold? (ii) How much pure gold is there in a 20 g ornament? (iii) Name the metals in brass and bronze. (iv) Why does a galvanised gate not rust even when scratched?
items.answer: (i) 83.3%. (ii) 16.7 g. (iii) Brass: copper and zinc; bronze: copper and tin. (iv) Zinc is more reactive and corrodes first, protecting iron.
